name: Rafael Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you start with a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach at Brookvale High, a secondary school in a market town, about 800 kids from the town and the villages around it. My timetable is half PE and half maths, which is a weird mix but it's what the school needed. Mornings are often maths with Year 8 and Year 9, afternoons are out on the field or in the sports hall. After school on Tuesdays and Thursdays I coach the Under-14 football team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the field, honestly. Kids who can't sit still in maths are different people with a ball. What's hard is the maths side; I'm not a natural maths teacher, my degree was sports science, and I'm still learning how to explain things like algebra to kids who've decided they hate it. I've started using an AI app now and then to give me three different ways to explain the same thing, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, so it's a handy tool and not much more. In the staffroom I'd shrug and go back to arguing about the football fixtures. I'm not big on posting things online about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. My job is secure, I've got a permanent contract, and I live on my own in a rented flat above a bakery, which is cheap. I've got about five months of money saved and I'm putting a bit away each month for a house deposit. In that world I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, and keep using the AI app to help with maths explanations when I'm stuck. I'd keep saving £250 a month for a deposit and maybe buy a place in three or four years. I'd also take my FA coaching badge next year, which I've been meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Bit boring, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in that world, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knee, if I'm honest. I did my cruciate playing rugby at uni, and on cold mornings out on the field it reminds me. If it went again, PE would be hard and I'd be all maths, which I'm not as good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's why I'm getting better at the maths side now, a bit of insurance. I'd rather be a decent maths teacher with a dodgy knee than a PE teacher who can't run. That's about the only planning I do.

say: I'd call AI a **handy tool** and not much more.
I'd shrug and get back to arguing about **football fixtures** in the staffroom.
think: My **permanent contract** and cheap flat make me feel secure.
With **five months** saved, I'd just carry on as before.
do: Keep using the **AI app** for maths explanations when stuck.
Save **£250 a month** towards a house deposit.
Take my **FA coaching badge** next year.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **boring**, which he's happy with.
S0.quote: I'd rather be a decent maths teacher with a dodgy knee than a PE teacher who can't run.
fieldNote: His only real worry here is his **knee**, not AI.
He's building the **maths side** as insurance against injury.
He uses AI casually, as a **second opinion** on explanations.

steps.text: Keep teaching half PE and half maths at Brookvale High
Save £250 a month towards a house deposit
Take the FA coaching badge next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for planning and marking, and that it won't be running a cross-country race with Year 7 in the rain any time soon. I'd say it half as a joke and half to make a point. People would probably agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the maths half of my job gets squeezed. If AI tutors can explain algebra better than me, and they probably can, the school might buy software for the weaker groups and give the maths lessons to the specialists. Then I'd be a PE teacher only, and a lot of schools only need one or two of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI app more seriously, every week instead of now and then, and get my maths teaching good enough to keep that half. I'd also offer to run more sports clubs, so they see me as the sport person. And I'd keep saving, maybe push the deposit plan back a year to have a bigger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but I'd be thinking about it on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the school keep you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being useful in both halves, I think. If I'm good with the tools in maths and I'm the one running the football and the athletics, I'm hard to lose. Our head likes teachers who take on extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push the house plan back a year. What's the real cost of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another year of renting above a bakery, so not the end of the world, it smells good at least. I'd rather wait than buy and then lose half my timetable. My dad lost his job at the paper mill the year after buying a bigger house, and I remember that.

say: I'd say AI won't run **cross-country with Year 7** any time soon.
I'd say it's good for **planning and marking**.
think: The **maths half** of my job could be squeezed by AI tutors.
Schools only need **one or two** PE teachers.
do: Use the **AI app weekly** to sharpen my maths teaching.
Push the **house purchase** back a year.
feel: **Uneasy**, thinking about it on the **drive in**.
S1.quote: My dad lost his job at the paper mill the year after buying a bigger house, and I remember that.
fieldNote: He sees **two halves** of his job with different risks.
His father's **redundancy** shapes how cautious he is with a house.
He plans to make himself **hard to lose** by taking on extra.

steps.text: Use the AI app every week to plan maths lessons
Offer to run extra athletics and football clubs
Delay buying a house by a year and keep saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to have a plan for schools and families, fast, because nobody would be ready. I'd say kids still need to move and play and be outside, and that a screen can't coach a football team. I'd post that, maybe, which I don't normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the maths half goes by 2028, because AI could teach it better than me and probably cheaper. The PE half is hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031, and honestly robots doing PE sounds daft, so maybe longer. But a lot of schools might cut PE hours if budgets got tight and everything changed at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the sport side now: coaching badges, maybe a level 3 qualification in sports coaching, around £600. I'd ask about running the school's after-school sport programme. I'd stop saving for a house and keep the cash for flexibility, and I'd talk to the local football club about paid coaching on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's my half-and-half job getting cut in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. In those three years I'd want to be the sport guy, fully, and maybe have coaching work outside school too. If robots can coach by 2031, then fair play, I don't know what anyone does, but I doubt it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older brother Gareth (a gym owner in the next town over) has always said I could do personal training at his place. I'd take him up on it at weekends, just to have another way in.

say: I'd ask for a **government plan** for schools and families, fast.
I'd say a **screen can't coach** a football team.
think: The **maths half** of my job goes by 2028.
**PE survives** to about 2031, though budgets could still cut it.
do: Do a **level 3 sports coaching** qualification for about £600.
Ask to run the school's **after-school sport** programme.
Do **weekend personal training** at my brother's gym.
feel: **Anxious**, watching his half-and-half job get **cut in half**.
S2.quote: My older brother Gareth (a gym owner in the next town over) has always said I could do personal training at his place.
fieldNote: He clearly separates his **thinking work** (maths) from his hands-on work (PE).
He treats 2028 to 2031 as a **window** to move fully into sport.
Family, through his **brother's gym**, is his backup.

steps.text: Pass a level 3 sports coaching qualification for about £600
Coach weekends for pay at the local football club
Do weekend personal training at Gareth's gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and I'd mean it. I'd tell the PE department we should be planning how sport fits in a world like that. Online, not much, same as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is decent for me. I'd do the coaching qualifications properly, get good, and by 2031 I'd be the person who runs sport at Brookvale. Maths still goes, I think, but I'd be ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the level 3 course over a year rather than cramming it. I'd keep saving for the house but keep a bigger emergency fund, six months instead of five. And I'd ask the head if I can drop maths gradually and take on more PE as the older PE teacher retires in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's like seeing a tackle coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of you that's relieved to lose the maths?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yeah, a bit. I've never loved it, I took it because the school needed it. If AI takes the maths and leaves me the field, I'd probably be happier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Then why still uneasy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's not just my job. My mates from school mostly work in offices, accounts and admin, and they'd be hit first. And I don't know how a town like ours copes if loads of people are out of work at once.

say: I'd say we've got **a few years**, so let's use them.
I'd ask the PE department to plan how **sport fits** in that world.
think: Five years lets me become the person who **runs sport** at Brookvale.
**Maths still goes**, but I'd be ready.
do: Do the **level 3 course** over a year.
Grow the emergency fund to **six months**.
Drop maths gradually as the **older PE teacher retires** in 2029.
feel: **Uneasy** but **in control**, like seeing a tackle coming.
S3.quote: If AI takes the maths and leaves me the field, I'd probably be happier.
fieldNote: He's partly **relieved** to lose the maths half.
His unease is about his **mates in offices** and his town.
Five years gives him a **clear succession** plan in PE.

steps.text: Take the level 3 sports coaching course over one year
Grow the emergency fund from five to six months
Move into full PE as the senior PE teacher retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out, if they start early. I'd encourage the Year 11s to think about it when choosing what to study. I'd say it calmly, because I'd feel fairly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, probably head of PE somewhere, and that's a hands-on job with three more years after that before robots. I'd worry about the town and about kids leaving school into a strange world. For me, I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a house, probably around 2029, once the coaching qualifications are done. I'd use AI tools more as they get better, especially for the paperwork side. And I'd go for head of PE as soon as it's open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Mostly I'd feel okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your Under-14s?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something with their hands or with people, not just a screen. And to keep playing sport, because being a good teammate is a skill no machine is going to take off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything else that would change for you with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably settle down. I'm single right now, but with ten years of steady work ahead I'd feel all right about a mortgage and maybe a family. With two years I'd keep everything loose.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to sort yourself out if you start early.
I'd tell Year 11 to think about it when **choosing what to study**.
think: By 2036 I'd likely be **head of PE**, with hands-on work lasting longer.
I'd worry about **the town** and about school leavers.
do: **Buy a house** around 2029 after finishing the coaching qualifications.
Use **AI for paperwork** as the tools improve.
Apply for **head of PE** when it opens.
S4.quote: Being a good teammate is a skill no machine is going to take off you.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him commit to a **mortgage** and maybe a family.
His leftover worry is **civic**, about his town and pupils.
He advises pupils towards **hands and people** work.

steps.text: Buy a house in the market town around 2029
Use AI tools for PE department paperwork
Plan to settle down and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't long to get qualified and change what you do, and if schools panicked they'd cut everything that isn't English and maths, PE included. What would help is the government keeping PE and sport protected in the timetable, and some funding for teachers to retrain into coaching and wellbeing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about kids' health. If everything goes to screens, someone has to make sure kids still move. That's not a small thing.

headlineQuote: If everything goes to screens, someone has to make sure kids still move.
portrait: Rafael is a second-year teacher splitting his week between **PE and maths** at a market-town secondary.
He lives alone in a **cheap flat**, has five months saved, and is saving for a house.
He sees **maths as exposed** and PE as safe, and is partly relieved to lose maths.
His mood stays **calm to anxious**, peaking in 2028 when time to retrain runs short.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **two years** is short and schools might **cut PE**.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **PE protected** in the school timetable.
Funding for teachers to retrain into **coaching and wellbeing**.
